To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
hypoxia induces cortical edema and neuronal death associated with the up-regulation of CRF and CRFR1, AQP4, and ET-1.

high altitude hypoxia triggers cerebral edema by inducing the expression of corticotropic releasing factor (CRFR1) in the brain, which activates aquaporin- 4 (AQP 4), the water channel in astrocytes, resulting in cerebral edema.

hypobaric-hypoxic hypoxia triggers cerebral edema and apoptosis by up-regulation of CRFR1, AQP4, and ET-1 expression, and that CRFR1 signaling contributes to the up-regulation of AQP4 expression and water influx in astrocytes, thereby inducing cerebral edema.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which CRFR1 and its downstream signaling contribute to cerebral edema.
the mechanisms underlying high-altitude cerebral edemas.
the mechanisms of hypobaric hypoxic cerebral edema.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

hypoxia triggers the release of CRF in the cortex, and the CRF, acting on the CRFR1, activates signaling of cAMP-PKA in cortical astroocytes to induce AQP4 expression and activation, and thereby produces cerebral edema.
hypobaric-hypoxic hypoxia-induced cerebral edema results from up-regulation of AQP4 by overactivation of CRF and its receptor CRFR1 in the brain.

hypoxia induces cortical edema by increasing the expression of CRF, CRFR1, AQP4, and ET-1, and that this process is mediated by the up-regulation of AQP4 expression by CRF, acting on CRFR1 in cortical astrocyte cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hypoxia induces cortical edema via the up-regulated expression of CRFR1 and ET-1 in astrocytes, which triggers signaling of c-AMP/PKA and intracellular Ca2+ and activates AQP4.
hypoxia induces CRF release, which activates CRFR1 to induce AQP4 expression and water influx into astroglial cells to produce edema.

hypobaric/hypoxic hypoxia induces cortical edema and neuronal cell death, which can be prevented by a CRFR1 antagonist, and that the mechanism of hypobaric/hypoic hypoxia-induced cerebral edema involves activation of CRFR1 and the subsequent up-regulation of AQP4 expression in astrocytes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hypoxia induces cortical release of CRFR1, which acts on astrocytic CRFR1 to activate AQP4 and contribute to cerebral edema.
hypoxia induces cortical release of CRFR1 and ET-1, both of which act to trigger signaling of AQP4 in cortical astrocyte to produce cerebral edema.
CRFR1 is a target for preventing cerebral edema.
